en: Dīgha Nikāya 28:
The Discourse on Full Confidence (Sampasādanīya Sutta) 1.
The Lion’s Roar of Sāriputta
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:

“Bhante, I am so confident in the Blessed One that there has never been, will never be, nor is there now another ascetic or brahmin who is more highly accomplished in regard to full enlightenment than the Blessed One.
“Sāriputta, this is a magnificent, bull-like utterance you have spoken; you have taken a definitive stand and let out a lion’s roar:
‘Bhante, I am so confident in the Blessed One...’”
"Nor has there been, nor will there be, nor is there now found another ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to this supreme enlightenment.

What do you think, Sāriputta? As for those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past—did you come to know all those Blessed Ones by encompassing their minds with your own mind, thinking:
"Those Blessed Ones had such virtue," or "Those Blessed Ones had such Dhamma," or "Those Blessed Ones had such wisdom"?
“Did those Blessed Ones exist? Did those Blessed Ones dwell in such a way?
Were those Blessed Ones liberated in such a way?”—“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“But, Sāriputta, have you encompassed with your mind the minds of all those who will be in the future time—those who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones—and known of them:
‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such virtue,’ and likewise, ‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such Dhamma… of such wisdom… of such conduct… of such liberation’?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“But, Sāriputta, have you now, by encompassing my mind with your own mind, understood me as I am—now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One—in this way:
‘The Blessed One is of such virtue, such is his Dhamma, such is his wisdom, such is his conduct, such is his liberation’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Moreover, Sāriputta, you do not possess the knowledge of others' minds regarding the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Then why, Sāriputta, have you uttered this sublime and bull-like speech, taken up a single position, and roared this lion’s roar:

‘Lord, I am so confident in the Blessed One that there has been, will be, or is now no other ascetic or brahmin who possesses greater direct knowledge than the Blessed One, namely, with respect to full enlightenment’?”
“Venerable sir, I do not possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Nevertheless, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.
Venerable sir, it is just as if there were a king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, strong walls and arches, and a single gate.
There, its gatekeeper would be wise, competent, and intelligent—one who keeps out strangers and admits those he knows.
As he walked along the patrol path surrounding that city, he would not see any joint in the wall nor any opening in the wall, not even one large enough for a cat to slip through.
He would think to himself:
‘Whatever gross beings enter or exit this city, all of them enter or exit through this very gate.
In the same way, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma has been understood by me:
All those Blessed Ones who were Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas in the past... [were all like this].”
Having abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— and with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
they developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are and fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And those, venerable sir, who will be in the future time, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones— all those Blessed Ones [will do likewise].
Having abandoned the five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, they will awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One, bhante, who is now an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, having abandoned the five hindrances—
those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— and having established his mind well in the four foundations of mindfulness,
has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by developing the seven factors of awakening as they truly are.
"Here, Bhante, I approached the Blessed One to hear the Dhamma.
To me, Bhante, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma—progressively higher and more sublime, dealing with the contrast between the dark and the bright.
Just as the Blessed One taught me the Dhamma progressively higher and more sublime, dealing with the contrast between the dark and the bright..."
In this way, through direct knowledge of that Dhamma, I reached a definitive conclusion regarding certain phenomena among all phenomena; I gained confidence in the Teacher, thinking:
"The Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of disciples has practiced rightly.
1.1. The Teaching on Wholesome Phenomena.
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states.
Therein, these are the wholesome states, namely:

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases for spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

"Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among wholesome states.
The Blessed One fully understands that; there is nothing further to be understood beyond what the Blessed One has fully understood."
"By which I recognize that no other ascetic or brahmin could be more distinguished than the Blessed One regarding wholesome states.
"Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the designations of the sense bases (*āyatana-pannatti*)."
"Venerable sir, there are these six internal and external sense bases:
the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the designations of sense bases."

The Blessed One knows that without remainder; for the Blessed One who knows that without remainder, there is nothing further to be directly known such that another ascetic or brahmin, by knowing it, might be more distinguished in direct knowledge than the Blessed One regarding the designations of the sense bases.
1.3. The Teaching on Descent into the Womb.
"Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed, in that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the descents into the womb.
There are these four descents into the womb, Bhante.

Here, Bhante, a certain person enters the mother’s womb without full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and departs from the mother’s womb without full awareness. This is the first descent into the womb."

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and departs from the mother’s womb without full awareness. This is the second descent into the womb.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness, and departs from the mother’s womb without full awareness. This is the third descent into the womb.
Furthermore, Bhante, here someone descends into the mother’s womb with full awareness; remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness; and emerges from the mother’s womb with full awareness.
This is the fourth mode of descent into the womb. This, Bhante, is unsurpassed among modes of descent into the womb. 1.4. Modes of Direct Address ... [The Buddha continued: ...

"Furthermore, Bhante, here a certain person, having approached a person of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, of such-and-such a caste, of such-and-such a livelihood, who eats such-and-such food, and who experiences such-and-such pleasure and pain, directly addresses them thus: ‘I know you, good man; I understand you, good man. Others say: ‘That is impossible, that cannot be; for how could anyone know another person, or understand them? Yet it is possible, Bhante, that one might know and understand another person in this way. This, Bhante, is unsurpassed among the modes of direct address."
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed, namely, the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the modes of direct knowledge (*ādesanā-vidhā*).
There are these four modes of direct knowledge, Bhante.
Here, Bhante, one person declares by means of a sign (*nimitta*): [text continues]
‘Such is your mind, such is your mind, such is your consciousness.
Even if he describes much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
This is the first method of direct address.
Furthermore, Bhante, here someone does not indeed predict by means of signs. Rather, having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, he predicts:
"Such is your mind, such is your mind, such is your thought.
Even if he predicts much, it happens exactly so and not otherwise.
This is the second method of direct declaration.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone does not declare [the future] by means of a sign, nor does he declare it after hearing the voice of humans, non-humans, or deities; rather, while he is thinking and reflecting...
Having heard the sound produced by the movement of his thoughts, he declares:
"Such is your mind, such is your intention, such is your consciousness.
Even if he declares much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
This is the third mode of direct declaration.
Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain person does not declare [the mind] by means of a sign,
nor does he declare it after hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, nor does he declare it from the sound produced by the diffusion of thought while one is thinking and deliberating.
Having heard it, he declares it. Moreover, having entered upon a concentration that is without applied thought and without sustained thought, he understands with his own mind the mind of another:
"In accordance with how this venerable one’s mental formations are directed, so will he apply such-and-such a thought immediately following this state of consciousness.
Even if he declares much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
This is the fourth mode of direct knowledge.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the modes of direct knowledge.
1.5. The Teaching on the Attainment of Vision.
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed, in that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the attainments of vision.
There are these four, Bhante, attainments of vision.
Here, Bhante, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through exertion, and through application...
By means of diligence and by means of right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he contemplates this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;
heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine.’
This is the first attainment of vision.
Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor...

[as before] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he directs his attention to this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward.
He contemplates it, bounded by the skin and full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... [and so on] ...lymph, urine.
And having gone beyond a man's skin, flesh, and blood, he contemplates the bone.
This is the second attainment of vision.
Furthermore, venerable sir, here some ascetic or brahmin, through ardor...

[as before] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he directs his attention to this very body from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward.
He contemplates it as filled to its very limits with various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... [and so on] ... lymph, urine.
And having gone beyond the skin, flesh, and blood of a man, he contemplates the bone.
And he understands the stream of consciousness of a person as uninterrupted on both sides, established both in this world and in the world beyond.
This is the third attainment of vision.
Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor … [as before] … such a state.

He attains concentration of mind; with his mind thus concentrated, he contemplates this very body from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... [and so on] ... grease, urine."
And having gone beyond the skin, flesh, and blood of a person, he contemplates the bone.
He understands the stream of consciousness of that person as uninterrupted on both sides, neither established here in this world nor established in the world beyond.
This is the fourth attainment of vision.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the attainments of vision.
Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the designations of persons.
"There are these seven persons, venerable sir:
one liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, and a faith-follower.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the designations of persons."
1.7. The Teaching on Exertion Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding exertions.

There are these seven factors of enlightenment, venerable sir: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the modes of striving. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, namely,
how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the ways of practice.
"These four, venerable sir, are the modes of practice: painful practice with slow direct knowledge,
painful practice with quick direct knowledge,
pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge," [and so forth].
"The pleasant way with quick direct knowledge.
In this regard, venerable sir, that practice which is painful with sluggish direct knowledge is declared inferior for both reasons: because of its painfulness and because of its sluggishness.
In this regard, venerable sir, that practice which is painful with quick direct knowledge is declared inferior because of its painfulness.
In this regard, venerable sir, that path which is pleasant with sluggish direct knowledge is declared inferior, venerable sir, because of its sluggishness.
But that path which is pleasant with swift direct knowledge, venerable sir, is declared superior for both reasons: because of its pleasantness and because of its swiftness.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among paths.

1.9. Instruction on Discourse Conduct and Other Matters Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding discourse conduct. Here, venerable sir, a certain person does not utter speech associated with false speech, nor divisive speech, nor slanderous speech, nor speech born of aggression while seeking victory; rather, he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is factual, speaks what is meaningful, speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and his speech is loved and welcomed by both gods and humans. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding discourse conduct. May the Blessed One accept this as unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding discourse conduct. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind. Here, venerable sir, a certain person, having abandoned covetousness for the world, dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and kind toward all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, no longer perplexed regarding wholesome qualities; he purifies his mind from doubt. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind. May the Blessed One accept this as unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of wisdom. Here, venerable sir, a certain person dwells contemplating the nature of impermanence in the body, perceiving the body as impermanent; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of suffering in the body, perceiving the body as suffering; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of non-self in the body, perceiving the body as non-self; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of repulsiveness in the body, perceiving the body as repulsive; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of dispassion in the body, perceiving the body as dispassionate; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of cessation in the body, perceiving the body as subject to cessation; he purifies his mind from lust for the body. He dwells contemplating the nature of impermanence in feelings, perceiving feelings as impermanent; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of suffering in feelings, perceiving feelings as suffering; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of non-self in feelings, perceiving feelings as non-self; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of repulsiveness in feelings, perceiving feelings as repulsive; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of dispassion in feelings, perceiving feelings as dispassionate; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of cessation in feelings, perceiving feelings as subject to cessation; he purifies his mind from lust for feelings. He dwells contemplating the nature of impermanence in the mind, perceiving the mind as impermanent; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of suffering in the mind, perceiving the mind as suffering; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of non-self in the mind, perceiving the mind as non-self; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of repulsiveness in the mind, perceiving the mind as repulsive; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of dispassion in the mind, perceiving the mind as dispassionate; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of cessation in the mind, perceiving the mind as subject to cessation; he purifies his mind from lust for the mind. He dwells contemplating the nature of impermanence in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as impermanent; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. He dwells contemplating the nature of suffering in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as suffering; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. He dwells contemplating the nature of non-self in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as non-self; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. He dwells contemplating the nature of repulsiveness in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as repulsive; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. He dwells contemplating the nature of dispassion in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as dispassionate; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. He dwells contemplating the nature of cessation in mental phenomena, perceiving mental phenomena as subject to cessation; he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of wisdom. May the Blessed One accept this as unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of wisdom. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind and the practice of wisdom. Here, venerable sir, a certain person, having abandoned covetousness for the world... [as above] ...he purifies his mind from lust for mental phenomena. Then, with his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he applies and directs his mind to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and evolution: "There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind and the practice of wisdom. May the Blessed One accept this as unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind and the practice of wisdom. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind and the practice of wisdom. Here, venerable sir, a certain person, with his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, applies and directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: "These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and performed actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. But these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views, and performed actions based on right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of the higher mind and the practice of wisdom. May the Blessed One accept this as unsurpassed in the way the
"Being wise, one speaks words that are measured and timely.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the practice of speech.
Furthermore, venerable sir, there is this other unsurpassed quality: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the practice of virtue for a person."
"Here, venerable sir, a certain person is truthful and faithful; he is not a deceiver, nor a boaster, nor one who hints, nor one who belittles, nor one who seeks gain with gain;

he guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, acts with impartiality, is devoted to the practice of wakefulness, is untiring, possesses aroused energy, and is a meditator endowed with mindfulness."
He is possessed of beautiful eloquence, he is resourceful, steadfast, and wise; he is not greedy for sensual pleasures, and he is mindful and prudent.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in the conduct of human virtue.
1.10. The Teaching on the Manner of Instruction.
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed, in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the methods of instruction.
There are these four methods of instruction, Bhante:
the Blessed One knows another person directly through careful attention.

‘This person, practicing according to the instruction, will, through the total destruction of the three fetters, become a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.
Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through careful attention:
‘This person, practicing according to the instruction, will, through the total destruction of the three fetters and the fading away of lust, hatred, and delusion…’
“With the thinning [of the fetters], he will become a once-returner; having come back to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering.
Venerable sir, through careful attention directed inwardly, the Blessed One knows another person:

“This person, practicing according to the instruction, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, will be of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.”
“Venerable sir, by means of careful attention directed inwardly, the Blessed One knows another person:

‘This person, practicing according to the instruction, will—through the destruction of the taints—realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, will dwell therein.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the methods of instruction.”

1.11. The Teaching on the Knowledge of the Liberation of Other Persons Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the knowledge of the liberation of other persons.

Venerable sir, through individual and thorough attention, the Blessed One knows another person: [thus he knows: "This person has such a nature, such a disposition, and such a character; his faculties are thus developed, and his defilements are thus attenuated. Thus he knows another person individually and thoroughly.

‘This person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, will become a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person by means of his own individual and thorough attention:

‘This person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, will become a once-returner; having come back to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering.’
“Venerable sir, through careful attention directed inwardly, the Blessed One knows another person:
‘This person, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, will be of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
Venerable sir, through careful attention directed inwardly, the Blessed One knows another person:”
‘This person, through the destruction of the taints, will, in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, realize for himself and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed regarding the knowledge of the liberation of other persons.
1.12. The Teaching on the Doctrine of Eternalism (Sassatavāda)
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed, in that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the doctrines of eternalism.
There are these three doctrines of eternalism, Bhante.
Here, Bhante, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor... [as before] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past lives.
That is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, and many hundreds of thousands of births.
“Many hundreds of thousands of births as well: ‘In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;

passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.’”
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
He says this:
“I know the past period—that the world contracted or that it expanded.”
"I know the future time: that the world will either contract or expand.

The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar. These beings run on and wander about, passing away and being reborn, yet they remain exactly as they are for all eternity.
This is the first doctrine of eternalism.

Furthermore, Bhante, here some ascetic or brahmin, through ardor … [as before] … attains such a state of mental concentration that, with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past abodes.

That is to say: one eon of dissolution and evolution, two eons of dissolution and evolution, three eons of dissolution and evolution, four eons of dissolution and evolution, five eons of dissolution and evolution, ten eons of dissolution and evolution: ‘There I was…’
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.
He says this:
"I know of the past time whether the world was contracting or expanding."
"I know the future time: that the world will either contract or expand.
The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
These beings run on and wander about, passing away and being reborn, yet they remain exactly as they are for all eternity."
This is the second doctrine of eternalism.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here some ascetic or brahmin, through ardor... [as before] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past lives.
That is to say: ten eons of world-dissolution and evolution, twenty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, thirty eons of world-dissolution and evolution.
Even forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, [he recollects]:

"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose in another place;
there too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
‘Having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
He says this:
“I know that in the past the world contracted and expanded.”
"I know the future time: the world will contract and the world will expand.
The self and the world are eternal, barren, fixed as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
And those beings run on and wander about, passing away and being reborn; yet they remain just so for all eternity."
This is the third doctrine of eternalism;
this, venerable sir, is the unsurpassed among the doctrines of eternalism.
1.13. The Teaching on the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives.
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed regarding the Blessed One’s teaching on the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Here, Bhante, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor...

[as above] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past lives. That is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births...

[as above] ...ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and evolution; "There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had such a name... and so on, in detail, he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and particulars. This, Bhante, is unsurpassed regarding the Blessed One’s teaching on the knowledge of recollecting past lives. This, Bhante, is what we consider unsurpassed in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. And this is the second thing in this way. May the Blessed One accept it from us as being unsurpassed."
ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion,
and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion.
‘In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, one recollects one’s manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.
"Venerable sir, there are deities whose lifespan cannot be calculated by means of counting or reckoning;

nevertheless, he remembers in whichever state of existence he formerly dwelt—whether among those with form or those without form, whether among those with perception, those without perception, or those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
"Thus he recollects his manifold past lives, with their modes and details.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed regarding the knowledge of the recollection of past lives.
1.14. Teaching on the Knowledge of Passing Away and Rebirth.
Furthermore, Bhante, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
Here, Bhante, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor...
[as before] ...attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings.
He sees beings passing away and being reborn—
low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma, [knowing]: "These worthy beings, indeed,
were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind..."
They were possessed of these qualities: they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, on the other hand, were possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, and possessed of good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones; they hold right view and undertake actions based on right view.

With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, namely, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the various kinds of supernormal power.
“Venerable sir, there are these two kinds of supernormal powers:
there is, venerable sir, supernormal power that is subject to taints and accompanied by acquisitions, which is called ‘non-noble’;
there is, venerable sir, supernormal power that is without taints and without acquisitions, which is called ‘noble.’”
"And what, venerable sir, is that psychic power which is accompanied by taints, accompanied by acquisitions, and is called 'not noble'?

Here, venerable sir, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor … [as before] … attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, he experiences various kinds of psychic power:
being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he passes through walls."
He goes unhindered through a wall or through a mountain, as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water;
he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; and he touches and strokes with his hand these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic.
He touches and strokes with his hand; he exercises mastery over the body even as far as the Brahma-world.
This, venerable sir, is supernormal power that is subject to taints and accompanied by acquisitions; it is called “non-noble.
But what, venerable sir, is supernormal power that is without taints and without acquisitions, which is called “noble”?
"Here, bhante, if a bhikkhu wishes: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive.
If he wishes: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive."
If he wishes: “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes: “May I, having set aside both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,” he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This, venerable sir, is a supernormal power that is taintless, free from acquisitions, and is called “noble.”
This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed among the various forms of psychic power.

The Blessed One fully understands this without exception; and for one who fully understands this without exception, there is no further higher knowledge to be attained such that another ascetic or brahmin, by understanding it, could surpass the Blessed One in regard to these various forms of psychic power.

1.16. Seeing the Teacher’s Qualities Otherwise “Venerable sir, that which is to be attained by a clansman endowed with faith—one who has aroused energy, who possesses fortitude, human strength, human vigor, human prowess, and human endurance—that has been attained by the Blessed One.
Yet, venerable sir, the Blessed One does not devote himself to the pursuit of sensual pleasure, which is low, vulgar, worldly, and common.”
He did not pursue the ignoble and unbeneficial practice of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
And the Blessed One was one who obtained at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
1.17. The Manner of Bestowing Practice
“Venerable sir, if one were to ask me:

‘Friend Sāriputta, were there in the past any other recluses or brahmins who were more highly accomplished in direct knowledge than the Blessed One?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘No. And if one were to ask me:

‘But friend Sāriputta, will there be in the future any other recluses or brahmins who will be more highly accomplished in direct knowledge than the Blessed One?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘No.’”

“But, friend Sāriputta, when asked: ‘Is there now any other ascetic or brahmin who is more highly accomplished in direct knowledge than the Blessed One regarding full enlightenment?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘No.
But if, venerable sir, one were to ask me:
‘Were there in the past any other ascetics or brahmins who were equal to the Blessed One regarding full enlightenment?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘Yes.’”

“But, friend Sāriputta, if I were asked: ‘Will there be, in the future, other recluses or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in regard to full enlightenment?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘Yes.
But if I were asked: ‘Are there, friend Sāriputta, at present other recluses or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in regard to full enlightenment?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would say ‘No.
Furthermore, venerable sir, if someone were to ask me this:”
“If I am asked, ‘But why does the Venerable Sāriputta approve of some things and not approve of others?’—being thus questioned, Bhante, I would answer:
‘Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, I have received it directly from him:
“In the past, there were Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, who were exactly equal to me in regard to enlightenment.”’”
"Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from him:
'In a future time, there will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, equal to me in regard to enlightenment.
Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from him."
“It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system; such a thing is not possible.

Venerable sir, if I were asked this and answered thus, would I be speaking in accordance with what was said by the Blessed One, would I not misrepresent the Blessed One with falsehood, would I be explaining in conformity with the Dhamma, and would there be no one who could rightly refute me?
“Does a legitimate discussion and counter-discussion lead to a ground for censure?
“Indeed, Sāriputta, when you are asked thus and answer in this way, you speak exactly as I have spoken;
you do not misrepresent me with what is false, you explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma [can find fault].”
“Argument and counter-argument lead to a ground for censure.
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One: [The section on] The Marvelous and Wonderful. Thus it was said, the Venerable Udāyī addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How great is the Tathāgata’s fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity!
For although the Tathāgata is so powerful and so mighty, yet he does not display himself.

Venerable sir, if even one of these qualities were found in the wanderers of other sects, they would carry a banner proclaiming it all over the country. But since they do not possess even a single one of them, they remain hidden away.”
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! Such is the Tathāgata’s fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity.
For even though the Tathāgata is so powerful and so mighty, he will not display himself.
“Behold, Udāyin, the Tathāgata’s fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity!”
"For indeed, although the Tathāgata is so powerful and so majestic, he will not yet reveal himself.
Udāyin, if even one single teaching from this [Dhamma] were to be found within themselves by the wanderers of other sects, they would carry a banner on that account alone.
Behold, Udāyin, the fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity of the Tathāgata!
"For indeed, the Tathāgata is so powerful and so majestic, yet he will not manifest himself.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Therefore, Sāriputta, you should frequently recite this discourse on the Dhamma for the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen."

"For even those foolish men, Sāriputta, who may have doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata, their doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata will be abandoned upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma.
Thus, in the presence of the Blessed One, the Venerable Sāriputta proclaimed his confidence.
Therefore, "inspiring confidence" is indeed the designation for this exposition.
The Sampasādanīya Sutta, the fifth, is finished.
